questions.question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.

Frivolous
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **Trivial**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The word **"frivolous"** means something that is not serious or lacks any real purpose or value. (तुच्छ, महत्वहीन)

 
 
• **Example:** She was criticised for spending money on **frivolous** items instead of saving for necessities.
 
 
 
• **"Trivial"** refers to something of little importance or value, often associated with insignificant matters. (सामान्य, मामूली)
 
 
• **Example:** The meeting wasted too much time discussing **trivial** issues instead of focusing on the key agenda.
 
 
 
• Hence, the synonym of **'frivolous'** is **'trivial'**.

Therefore, the correct answer is: **Trivial**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

Here are the other options explained along with their Hindi meanings and example sentences:

 
• **Substantial** (महत्वपूर्ण): Refers to something of considerable importance, size, or worth.

 
 
• **Example:** The company made **substantial **progress in reducing its carbon footprint.
 
 
 
• **Momentous** (महत्वपूर्ण): Refers to something of great significance or importance, particularly in historical or future contexts.
 
 
• **Example:** The signing of the peace treaty was a **momentous **event in history.
 
 
 
• **Eventful** (घटनापूर्ण): Refers to something full of interesting or important events.
 
 
• **Example:** It was an **eventful **day, filled with surprises and celebrations.

questions.question:
The given sentence is divided into four segments. Select the option that has the segment with an adverbial usage error.

Oliver told Mia, "Seldom than walking, she prefers to take the city bus."
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The adverbial usage error lies in the phrase **"Seldom than walking."**
 
• The correct phrase should be **"Seldom walking"** or **"Rather than walking."**
 
• The word **"seldom"** is an adverb and is used to indicate infrequent actions, but it should not be followed by "than."
 
• "Than" is used for comparisons, which is incorrect in this context.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"Oliver told Mia, 'Seldom walking, she prefers to take the city bus.'"*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: "take the city bus."** – This part of the sentence is grammatically correct and does not require any changes.
 
• **Option 2: "she prefers to"** – This part of the sentence is grammatically correct and does not require any changes.
 
• **Option 3: "Oliver told Mia,"** – This part of the sentence is grammatically correct and does not require any changes.

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate idiom that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

She didn't want to __upset anyone__ at work, so she carefully navigated the office politics.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is: **Option 1** i.e., **step on anyone's toes**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The phrase **"upset anyone"** means to cause someone to feel troubled, annoyed, or offended. (किसी को नाराज़ करना)

 
 
• **Example:** He avoided talking about politics so as not to **upset anyone** at the party.
 
 
 
• **"Step on anyone's toes"** is an idiom which means to offend someone by interfering in their affairs or responsibilities. (किसी के अधिकार क्षेत्र में हस्तक्षेप करना या उसे नाराज़ करना)
 
 
• **Example:** She made sure not to **step on anyone’s toes** while introducing new policies in the office.
 
 
 
• This idiom perfectly replaces "**upset anyone**" in the sentence, as both convey the idea of avoiding conflict or offense.

Therefore, the correct answer is: **step on anyone's toes**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

Here are the other options explained along with their Hindi meanings and example sentences:

 
• **Bite the bullet** (कठिन परिस्थिति को सहना): To bravely face or endure an unpleasant situation.

 
 
• **Example:** I had to **bite the bullet** and tell my boss the truth about the mistake.
 
 
 
• **Steal the show** (सबका ध्यान खींच लेना): To receive more attention or praise than anyone else in a performance or event.
 
 
• **Example:** The little boy in the dance group **stole the show** with his amazing moves.
 
 
 
• **Scratch anyone's heads** (किसी को उलझन में डालना): This is not a standard idiom. The correct version is usually "scratch one's head," which means to feel confused or puzzled.
 
 
• **Example:** The strange question made everyone **scratch their heads** in confusion.

The COVID-19 pandemic led to trade disruptions worldwide, but the agricultural and food sector __prove to more resilient__ than other sectors of the economy.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 4**.

__
 
• The original sentence contains a tense-related error in the phrase "**prove to more resilient**."
 
• Since the sentence refers to a completed action in the past (during the COVID-19 pandemic), the correct tense should be the past tense "**proved**."
 
• The correct phrase is "**proved to be more resilient**," which aligns with the past context of the sentence.
 
• Thus, the correct option is **Option 4**, as it ensures both grammatical correctness and appropriate verb tense usage.

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"The COVID-19 pandemic led to trade disruptions worldwide, but the agricultural and food sector **proved to be more resilient** than other sectors of the economy."*

• **Option 2: "proved to been more resilient" **– This is incorrect because "been" is unnecessary and grammatically incorrect in this context.
 
• **Option 3: "proving to be more resilient" **– This is incorrect because "proving" is in the present continuous tense, which does not fit the past context of the sentence.
